key_insight: In low-dimensional pnictogen chalcohalides, the most stable surface facets can still differ in band-edge alignment by up to 0.8 eV, making surface orientation a major hidden driver of solar-cell performance.
engineering_relevance: Controlling crystal facet exposure at absorber/contact interfaces could improve charge extraction and reduce open-circuit-voltage losses in MChX photovoltaics.
method: First-principles calculations of surface energetics across Bi/Sb, S/Se, and I/Br compounds
Exhaustive facet sampling including low-symmetry orientations to identify stable terminations
Drift-diffusion device modeling to translate surface energetics into solar-cell voltage losses
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that (011) and (010) are the most stable surfaces in all eight compounds, with only ~0.01–0.03 J m^-2 formation-energy differences but up to 0.8 eV band-edge shifts, and BiSBr simulations showing as much as a 0.6 V Voc drop.
watch_item: These results are strongly orientation-dependent and model-based, so real devices may vary with surface reconstruction, defects, and contact chemistry.
paper_title: Surface Physics of Low-Dimensional Pnictogen Chalcohalides and Its Impact on Photovoltaic Technologies
